{"title":"Introducing Python Virtual Environments","body":"Begin by reminding the class that the Django blog tutorial will soon ask them to install different package versions for different projects. Point out that without isolation, upgrading one library can break another, as the text on page 47 warns. Explain that a virtual environment is simply a folder that contains its own Python interpreter and its own site‑packages directory, so whatever you install there stays there and does not affect the system Python. Show the two one‑line commands from the book – on Linux/macOS `python -m venv my_env` and on Windows `py -m venv my_env` – and note that the only difference is the launcher used.

Tell the teacher to have students run the appropriate command, then activate the environment (`source my_env/bin/activate` or `my_env\Scripts\activate`) and observe that `pip list` now shows an empty set of third‑party packages. This concrete experience makes the abstract idea of isolation click, because they can see that installing a package inside the env does not appear in the global interpreter.

Finally, connect the skill to the upcoming step in the blog project where they will install Django and other dependencies from a requirements file. Emphasize that each project will get its own env, preventing the version‑conflict scenario described on page 47, and that later chapters will rely on this pattern when configuring separate development and production settings.

Check question: “What exact command does the book tell you to run on Windows to create a virtual environment called my_env?” If a student can recite `py -m venv my_env` you know the prerequisite is in place."}
